title: Problem 08
markdown:
### Problem
The coefficients $a_j$ in the polynomial $P(x) = a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n$ are integers satisfying $0 \le a_j \le 10$ and $a_n > 0$. If $P(1) = 21$ and $P(11) = 2011$, determine, with proof, the value of $P(6)$.

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
We show that $P(6) = 441$.

Because $0 \le a_j \le 10$, evaluating $P(11)$ is equivalent to writing 2011 in base 11:

$$2011 = a_n \cdot 11^n + \dots + a_1 \cdot 11 + a_0.$$

Since base 11 representations are unique:
- $2011 \div 11 = 182$ remainder $9 \implies a_0 = 9$
- $182 \div 11 = 16$ remainder $6 \implies a_1 = 6$
- $16 \div 11 = 1$ remainder $5 \implies a_2 = 5$
- $1 \div 11 = 0$ remainder $1 \implies a_3 = 1$.

Thus $P(x) = x^3 + 5x^2 + 6x + 9$.

Notice that $P(1) = 1 + 5 + 6 + 9 = 21$, which confirms consistency.

Finally, evaluate at $x = 6$:

$$P(6) = 6^3 + 5(6^2) + 6(6) + 9 = 216 + 180 + 36 + 9 = 441.$$

### Conceptual Explanation
The condition $0 \le a_j \le 10$ means the polynomial coefficients are the unique base-11 digits of $P(11) = 2011$. Converting $2011_{10}$ to base 11 yields $(1569)_{11}$, giving $P(x) = x^3 + 5x^2 + 6x + 9$. Evaluating at $x = 6$ yields 441.

### Key Technique
Polynomial evaluation at an integer base matching coefficient bounds is identical to unique base-b positional expansion.
